title: Genetic Processes
standard_text: Meiosis and how it produces variation; Mendel's laws; monohybrid and dihybrid crosses; incomplete dominance, codominance, multiple alleles and sex-linked traits; pedigrees and genetic disorders; and genetic technologies. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Biology, Grade 11, University Preparation (SBI3U), Strand D: Genetic Processes)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Biology (SBI3U) worksheets on genetic processes: meiosis, Punnett squares, monohybrid and dihybrid crosses, incomplete dominance, blood types, sex-linked traits and biotechnology. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Each parent passes on one allele of each gene.
key_sub: A Punnett square shows the expected ratios of offspring.
body_html:
How to think about it

Meiosis makes gametes with half the number of chromosomes (23 in humans). Crossing over and independent assortment make every gamete different. At fertilization, the zygote gets one allele of each gene from each parent.

Write the parents' genotypes, list their gametes and fill in a Punnett square. A monohybrid cross of two heterozygotes (Aa × Aa) gives a 3 : 1 phenotype ratio; a dihybrid cross (AaBb × AaBb) gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. Not all traits follow simple dominance: incomplete dominance blends, codominance shows both, and X-linked traits appear more often in males.

Example

Aa × aa. What fraction of the offspring show the recessive trait?

Gametes: A, a and a, a

Offspring: Aa, Aa, aa, aa

Answer: 1/2

Example

A colour-blind man (XᵇY) and a woman who is not a carrier (XᴮXᴮ). What fraction of their sons are colour-blind?

Sons get the X from their mother: Xᴮ

Answer: none

Common mistakes

  • Confusing genotype (letters) with phenotype (the trait).
  • Forgetting that each gamete carries only one allele of each gene.
  • Giving sons their X chromosome from the father.

faq.q: What is the difference between mitosis and meiosis?
faq.a: Mitosis makes two identical diploid cells; meiosis makes four different haploid gametes.
Both alleles are fully shown in the heterozygote, as in blood type AB.

items.q: In which stage of meiosis does this happen: chiasmata terminalize and the nuclear envelope breaks down?
items.e: Diakinesis: chiasmata terminalize and the nuclear envelope breaks down.

items.q: What happens in zygotene of meiosis?
c: chiasmata terminalize and the nuclear envelope breaks down
the synaptonemal complex dissolves and chiasmata are seen
homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) to form bivalents
homologous chromosomes separate while sister chromatids stay together
items.e: Zygotene: homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) to form bivalents.

items.q: A potato egg and sperm each have 24 chromosomes. How many does the fertilized egg have?
A horse cell (2n = 64) finishes meiosis I. How many chromosomes are in each of the two new cells?
items.e: Homologs separate in meiosis I, so each cell has 32 (each still with two chromatids).

items.q: Which stage of meiosis? Homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles.
items.e: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

items.q: What happens in leptotene of meiosis?
c: chromosomes become visible as thin threads
crossing over takes place at recombination nodules
chiasmata terminalize and the nuclear envelope breaks down
homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) to form bivalents
items.e: Leptotene: chromosomes become visible as thin threads.

items.q: Meiosis: main purpose?
items.e: Meiosis: making gametes for sexual reproduction. Mitosis: growth and repair.

items.q: In which stage of meiosis does this happen: homologous chromosomes separate while sister chromatids stay together?
items.e: Anaphase I: homologous chromosomes separate while sister chromatids stay together.

items.q: A fruit fly body cell has 8 chromosomes. How many homologous pairs is that?
items.e: 8 ÷ 2 = 4 pairs.

items.q: Which stage of meiosis? Four haploid cells are formed.
items.e: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

items.q: In which stage of meiosis does this happen: crossing over takes place at recombination nodules?
items.e: Pachytene: crossing over takes place at recombination nodules.

items.q: In which stage of meiosis does this happen: sister chromatids separate as the centromere splits?
items.e: Anaphase II: sister chromatids separate as the centromere splits.

items.q: Meiosis: crossing over happens?
items.e: Meiosis: yes. Mitosis: no.

items.q: What happens in diakinesis of meiosis?
c: homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) to form bivalents
sister chromatids separate as the centromere splits
chiasmata terminalize and the nuclear envelope breaks down
chromosomes become visible as thin threads
items.e: Diakinesis: chiasmata terminalize and the nuclear envelope breaks down.

items.q: Meiosis: chromosome number in new cells?
items.e: Meiosis: half (haploid). Mitosis: same (diploid).

items.q: Mitosis: crossing over happens?
items.e: Meiosis: yes. Mitosis: no.

items.q: Which stage of meiosis? Sister chromatids separate to opposite poles.
items.e: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

items.q: A horse body cell has 64 chromosomes (2n). How many are in each egg or sperm cell?
items.e: Meiosis halves the number: n = 32.

items.q: What is the significance of meiosis?
c: it halves the chromosome number for gametes and creates variation
items.e: Fertilization restores the diploid number.

items.q: Which stage of meiosis? Single chromosomes line up in the middle of two cells.
items.e: Meiosis I separates homologs; meiosis II separates sister chromatids.

items.q: In pea, tall (T) is dominant over dwarf (t). Two heterozygous tall plants (Tt × Tt) give 100 offspring. How many are expected to be tall?
items.e: Tt × Tt gives 3 tall : 1 dwarf, so ¾ of 100 = 75.

items.q: Cross: GG × Gg corn (green leaves dominant). What phenotype ratio do you expect?
items.e: Use a Punnett square.

items.q: A heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt) is test-crossed with a dwarf plant (tt), giving 56 offspring. How many are expected to be dwarf?
items.e: Tt × tt gives 1 tall : 1 dwarf: 28.

items.q: In pea, tall (T) is dominant over dwarf (t). Two heterozygous tall plants (Tt × Tt) give 180 offspring. How many are expected to be dwarf?
items.e: Tt × Tt gives 3 tall : 1 dwarf, so ¼ of 180 = 45.

items.q: What is aneuploidy?
c: the gain or loss of one or a few chromosomes
items.e: Polyploidy is an increase in whole sets.

items.q: What is linkage?
c: the tendency of genes on the same chromosome to be inherited together
items.e: Recombination happens when crossing over separates them.

items.q: A dihybrid RrYy is test-crossed with rryy, giving 96 offspring. How many are expected to be wrinkled and green?
items.e: The test-cross ratio is 1 : 1 : 1 : 1, so 24.

items.q: In snapdragon, flower colour shows incomplete dominance (RR red, Rr pink, rr white). A cross Rr × Rr gives 52 plants. How many are expected to be pink?
items.e: The ratio is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, so 26.

items.q: In pea, round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) over green (y). An RrYy × RrYy cross gives 448 seeds. How many are expected to be round and yellow?
items.e: The F₂ ratio is 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, so 9/16 of 448 = 252.

items.q: In snapdragons, two pink parents are crossed (incomplete dominance). What percent of offspring are pink?
items.e: 1 : 2 : 1, so 50% are pink.

items.q: ABO blood type: A and B are codominant, O is recessive. Parents' genotypes are I<sup>A</sup>i and I<sup>B</sup>I<sup>B</sup>. What is the chance of a child with type A blood?
items.e: Make a Punnett square and count type A.

items.q: What is the law of segregation?
c: the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation
items.e: Each gamete gets one allele.

items.q: A dihybrid RrYy is test-crossed with rryy, giving 88 offspring. How many are expected to be wrinkled and green?

items.q: In pea, round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) over green (y). An RrYy × RrYy cross gives 112 seeds. How many are expected to be round and green?

items.q: In tomato plants, the cross Aa × Aa is made. What proportion of the offspring show the recessive phenotype?
items.e: Draw a Punnett square for Aa × Aa and count the matching boxes: 14.

items.q: In four o'clock flowers, two pink parents are crossed (incomplete dominance). What percent of offspring are white?
items.e: 1 : 2 : 1, so 25% are white.

items.q: What is pleiotropy?
c: one gene affecting several characters, as in phenylketonuria
items.e: Polygenic inheritance is the reverse.

items.q: Who proposed the chromosomal theory of inheritance?
items.e: Genes are on chromosomes.

items.q: What causes Turner's syndrome?
c: lack of the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine
a protein needed for blood clotting is missing
a missing X chromosome in a female (XO)
a single base change making valine replace glutamic acid in β-globin
items.e: Turner's syndrome: a missing X chromosome in a female (XO).

items.q: Which mechanism of sex determination is found in humans and Drosophila?
items.e: Humans and Drosophila: XX–XY (male heterogametic).

items.q: Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. The mother is a carrier and the father is colour-blind. What is the chance a daughter is colour-blind?
items.e: Sons get their X from their mother; daughters get one X from each parent.

items.q: Which disorder is caused by an extra X chromosome in a male (XXY)?
items.e: Klinefelter's syndrome: an extra X chromosome in a male (XXY).

items.q: Which disorder is caused by a protein needed for blood clotting is missing?
items.e: Haemophilia: a protein needed for blood clotting is missing.

items.q: What causes Klinefelter's syndrome?
c: an extra X chromosome in a male (XXY)
a missing X chromosome in a female (XO)
lack of the enzyme that converts phenylalanine into tyrosine
items.e: Klinefelter's syndrome: an extra X chromosome in a male (XXY).

items.q: What causes hemophilia?
c: a missing X chromosome in a female (XO)
a protein needed for blood clotting is missing
an extra X chromosome in a male (XXY)
items.e: Haemophilia: a protein needed for blood clotting is missing.

items.q: Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. The mother is a carrier and the father is colour-blind. What is the chance a son is colour-blind?
items.e: Sons get their X from their mother; daughters get one X from each parent.

items.q: In which organisms is the sex determined by ZW–ZZ (female heterogametic)?
items.e: Birds: ZW–ZZ (female heterogametic).

items.q: In which organisms is the sex determined by haplodiploidy (males develop from unfertilized eggs)?
items.e: Honey bees: haplodiploidy (males develop from unfertilized eggs).

items.q: Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. The mother is not a carrier and the father is colour-blind. What is the chance a son is colour-blind?
items.e: Sons get their X from their mother; daughters get one X from each parent.

items.q: Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. The mother is a carrier and the father is not colour-blind. What is the chance a daughter is colour-blind?
items.e: Sons get their X from their mother; daughters get one X from each parent.

items.q: Which mechanism of sex determination is found in honey bees?

items.q: What causes Down's syndrome?

items.q: Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. The mother is not a carrier and the father is colour-blind. What is the chance a daughter is colour-blind?

items.q: Red-green colour blindness is X-linked recessive. The mother is a carrier and the father is not colour-blind. What is the chance a son is colour-blind?

items.q: In which organisms is the sex determined by XX–XO (male has one X)?

items.q: Which disorder is caused by an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21)?

items.q: In which organisms is the sex determined by XX–XY (male heterogametic)?

items.q: PCR starts with 100 DNA molecules. How many molecules are there after 25 cycles?
items.e: The DNA doubles each cycle: 100 × 225 = 3.36 × 109.

items.q: What is bioreactor?
c: separating and purifying the product before marketing
cutting out and recovering DNA bands from a gel
separating DNA fragments by size in an agarose gel
a large vessel in which cells are grown to make products
items.e: Bioreactor: a large vessel in which cells are grown to make products.

items.q: What is Bt cotton known for?
c: resisting bollworms with a toxin gene from Bacillus thuringiensis
the company that made human insulin from E. coli in 1983
producing milk rich in human α-lactalbumin
correcting a gene defect, as first done for ADA deficiency in 1990
items.e: Bt cotton: resisting bollworms with a toxin gene from Bacillus thuringiensis.

items.q: What is a vector?
c: a DNA molecule, such as a plasmid, that carries foreign DNA into a host cell
items.e: Plasmids and bacteriophages are vectors.

items.q: What is EcoRI?
c: a large vessel in which cells are grown to make products
separating and purifying the product before marketing
a bacterium that transfers T-DNA into plants
a restriction enzyme from Escherichia coli RY13 that cuts at GAATTC
items.e: EcoRI: a restriction enzyme from Escherichia coli RY13 that cuts at GAATTC.

items.q: Why is a promoter added with a gene in genetic engineering?
c: so RNA polymerase can bind and the gene is transcribed
items.e: A terminator is added to stop it.

items.q: Which term matches this description: staining DNA so it shows orange under UV light?
items.e: Ethidium bromide: staining DNA so it shows orange under UV light.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 4000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1100, 3750. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 4000): 2650, 1100, 250. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: Each PCR cycle takes 2 minutes. How many cycles can be completed in 40 minutes, and so how many times larger is the DNA amount?
items.e: 20 cycles; amount × 220 = 1048576.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 4000 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1100. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 4000): 2900, 1100. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 1200 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1000. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 1200): 1000, 200. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: Each PCR cycle takes 4 minutes. How many cycles can be completed in 100 minutes, and so how many times larger is the DNA amount?

items.q: A linear DNA molecule of 2400 base pairs is cut by a restriction enzyme at positions 1250, 1700, 2000. Which fragment sizes (bp) appear on the gel?
items.e: Subtract neighbouring positions (including 0 and 2400): 1250, 450, 400, 300. The smallest fragments move furthest on the gel.

items.q: What is Agrobacterium tumefaciens?

a restriction enzyme from Escherichia coli RY13 that cuts at GAATTC
inserting a gene into a marker so the marker stops working
staining DNA so it shows orange under UV light
items.e: Agrobacterium tumefaciens: a bacterium that transfers T-DNA into plants.

items.q: What does blue–white selection show?

items.e: Non-recombinants make β-galactosidase and turn blue.
